title: Cheap, scalable storage for weeks to seasons of electrical supply

concept.text: The innovation is an economical, broadly deployable way to store energy and later return it as controllable electricity over weeks or across seasons. It would combine inexpensive storage capacity with adequate conversion efficiency, long service life, dependable output, and materials and siting requirements that permit widespread deployment. The concept describes a desired capability, rather than a particular battery chemistry or storage mechanism.

Scope synthesis: weeks-long discharge and seasonal storage are separate requirements. The first concerns how long a system can sustain electricity delivery; the second concerns retaining energy across a long interval before delivering it. Demonstrating several days of output does not establish either weeks-long supply or economical seasonal shifting. A complete solution could involve electrochemical, mechanical, thermal, or fuel-based storage, provided the full process returns useful electricity and meets the economic and deployment requirements.

significance.text: If sufficiently cheap and scalable, storage spanning extended generation shortfalls could substantially change electricity-system design. It could allow variable generation to supply a greater share of electricity while stored energy provides dispatchable output during prolonged shortfalls. DOE’s July 2023 presentation links long-duration storage to renewable integration, resilience, and reduced requirements for new gas capacity. These are grounds for the innovation’s potential significance, rather than evidence that seasonal-scale performance or savings have been achieved.

System-level synthesis: the direct advance would be greater freedom to separate electricity generation from electricity consumption over long periods. Conditional downstream possibilities include different generation portfolios, less dependence on some backup resources, and improved resilience during extended low-generation conditions. Storage still requires charging energy, conversion equipment, and a network capable of delivering its output. It would neither eliminate transmission nor necessarily replace every other dispatchable resource, and its value would depend on regional resources, reliability requirements, and competing ways to meet demand.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central challenge is to combine very low cost per unit of stored energy with useful efficiency, lifetime, controllable power, and broad scalability. The supplied DOE presentation treats delivered cost, functional performance, materials sourcing, permitting, and siting as adoption factors, and identifies needs for cost reduction, efficiency improvements, manufacturing scale-up, and field demonstrations. Its comparison also identifies geological constraints relevant to storage deployment. These factors explain the development challenge but do not establish a comprehensive comparison of all seasonal-storage options.

Engineering synthesis: storage capacity and output power must be evaluated separately. A system needs enough usable energy to cover the intended interval and enough conversion capacity to deliver the required power. Seasonal operation additionally requires acceptable losses during storage, dependable restart and dispatch after long idle periods, and materials and equipment that tolerate the intended operating conditions. Which barrier dominates depends on the storage mechanism; the supplied evidence does not identify a single scientific discovery that would resolve every requirement.

Economic synthesis: inexpensive storage media alone would not establish inexpensive delivered electricity. Charging energy, conversion losses, power equipment, financing, maintenance, replacement, land, and material requirements all matter. Seasonal systems may spread their costs over relatively few charge-discharge cycles, making lifetime and utilization assumptions especially consequential. Short-duration batteries and geographically constrained pumped hydro illustrate why an existing storage capability does not automatically supply the entire weeks-to-seasons combination.

current_state.text: The supplied review identifies the retained DOE artifact as Vanessa Chan’s presentation at a July 27, 2023 summit, rather than the underlying Liftoff report. It describes long-duration storage technologies at differing readiness levels and calls for further field demonstrations, cost reductions, efficiency improvements, and manufacturing scale-up. This supports a dated account of technical and commercialization challenges. It does not establish deployment status as of November 1, 2026, or prove that the full capability remains unavailable.

The presentation’s taxonomy places short-duration storage at up to 10 hours and distinguishes multi-day/week discharge from seasonal shifting. Its stated focus excludes the separate seasonal-shifting category. Accordingly, its discussion of longer-duration technologies and projected system benefits cannot by itself establish cheap seasonal electricity storage. Multi-day progress is relevant, but evidence of discharge duration must be distinguished from evidence of retention across seasons and subsequent electricity delivery.

According to the supplied review, a saved copy of the presentation was identifiable and its extraction covered all 21 pages without declared truncation. The earlier account of a failed retrieval therefore does not describe the available evidence. However, the flattened extraction of the technology-comparison graphic does not reliably preserve every row or graphical association, so it cannot support precise technology-specific numerical comparisons. The earlier numerical estimates are not established by the supplied review and are not repeated here.

Evidence limitation: no inspectable evidence for the previously referenced 2025 iron-air pilot milestone, and no bounded search documenting subsequent developments, was supplied. That milestone cannot be treated here as a verified demonstration. This limitation does not show that the pilot failed to occur. The supplied material also does not establish an audited installation delivering the full weeks-to-seasons capability at broadly competitive cost.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently audited, grid-connected installations should operate for several years in contrasting climates, repeatedly sustain weeks-long discharge, and separately retain energy across seasons before returning it as electricity. Audits should report usable energy, controllable output, charging requirements, conversion and retention losses, degradation, maintenance, replacement, and material and siting requirements. Repetition across installations and operating conditions would establish demonstrated breadth and reproducibility, rather than literal applicability everywhere.
completion_criteria.label: Audited installations reproduce weeks-long discharge and seasonal electricity recovery

completion_criteria.text: Proposed economic test: disclosed lifecycle accounting should include charging energy, losses, financing, maintenance, replacement, land, and materials. Regional power-system studies should show that measured performance and defensible costs materially change least-cost grid designs in multiple regions under explicit reliability requirements and modeling assumptions. Comparisons should include relevant generation, transmission, demand-management, and storage alternatives. Several years of operation would still require justified extrapolations and sensitivity analysis for longer equipment lifetimes and replacement schedules.
completion_criteria.label: Full lifecycle accounting demonstrates least-cost grid changes across multiple regions

completion_criteria.text: These proposed criteria extend DOE’s commercialization framework, which emphasizes deployment at scale, cost and performance transparency, valuation tools, and project operating data. The presentation does not prescribe the proposed audit independence, climate diversity, operating duration, or full accounting boundary, and its narrower scope does not establish a seasonal-storage completion standard.
completion_criteria.label: DOE commercialization framework does not establish seasonal-storage completion standards

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ELE-09, Resilient, self-restoring power networks, has the closest system-level overlap. Long-duration storage could supply energy during extended disruptions or generation shortages, while a self-restoring network concerns detecting faults, reconfiguring service, and recovering operation. Stored energy can support resilience, but storage alone does not confer those network capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: ELE-01, Practical ambient-temperature superconducting conductors, and ELE-07, Infrastructure-scale wireless electrical power delivery, concern carrying electricity. ELE-05 concerns making energy available at a later time. Improvements in delivery could complement storage, but would not establish long-term retention, economical storage capacity, or weeks-long discharge; storage would likewise retain a need for suitable electrical connections.

Roster-based synthesis: ELE-04, Practical, energy-recovering reversible computing; ELE-08, Manufacturable ultra-low-voltage switching for general-purpose electronics; and ELE-11, Integrated photonic-electronic computing with broad system advantage, could affect electricity demand if their system benefits were realized. Such changes could alter storage requirements, but efficient computation and long-duration energy storage remain distinct capabilities. ELE-10, Broadly deployable, maintenance-free ambient-powered sensing, similarly concerns powering small distributed devices rather than supplying grid-scale electricity across weeks or seasons.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not resolve deployment status as of November 1, 2026; no bounded freshness search record was provided.
The previously referenced 2025 iron-air pilot milestone and earlier numerical estimates remain unverified. Their omission is not a finding that they are false.
Precise technology-specific comparisons cannot be reconstructed reliably from the flattened comparison graphic described in the review.
The supplied presentation does not provide a comprehensive seasonal-storage comparison or establish which pathway could meet the full cost, performance, lifetime, materials, and siting requirements.
Economically convincing cost and performance thresholds remain region-dependent and would require explicit reliability, utilization, financing, and lifetime assumptions.

brief.title: Affordable electricity stored for weeks and seasons
possible: Homes and businesses could draw on stored electricity through weeks of low wind or sunshine. Energy saved in a season of plentiful generation could also supply power in a later season.
why: Electricity systems could rely more on wind and solar while keeping power available during prolonged shortfalls. Cheap storage could reduce the need for new gas plants and help communities withstand extended disruptions.

sources.who: Vanessa Chan, U.S. Department of Energy
sources.showed: The presentation describes storage technologies at different stages of development and identifies barriers to widespread use, including cost, efficiency, manufacturing and suitable sites.
sources.cited_for: It explains what storage must overcome to become widely used.
sources.not_established: Its scope excludes seasonal shifting, and it does not demonstrate affordable seasonal electricity storage.

sources.who: Qiming Tang, Yongliang Zhang, Nansheng Xu, Xueling Lei and Kevin Huang
sources.showed: The team demonstrated repeated cycles in a laboratory battery that stores energy through reactions involving iron and oxygen.
sources.quote:
Here in this work, we
demonstrate that a laboratory size solid oxide iron–air battery can readily achieve long-duration cycles with high energy density and round-trip efficiency.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates laboratory progress toward longer electricity storage.
sources.not_established: The experiment does not establish weeks of output, seasonal retention or affordable operation at grid scale.

sources.showed: Their electricity-system model found that the value of storing electricity for long periods depends on regional generation and storage costs.
sources.quote: We find that a) LDES is particularly valuable in majority wind-powered regions and regions with diminishing hydropower generation,
sources.cited_for: It supports the case that storage value depends on the region.
sources.not_established: Modeled benefits do not demonstrate that a storage installation can achieve the assumed costs and performance.

sources.showed: Their model found that adding long-duration storage, meaning storage for extended periods, lowered costs in electricity systems supplied by wind and solar.
sources.quote:
Moreover, dependence on LDS
increases when the system is optimized over more years.
sources.cited_for: It shows why electricity planning must account for weather variations across years.
sources.not_established: The study models storage roles and costs; it does not demonstrate a working seasonal storage system.

shown: Tang and colleagues achieved repeated 12.5-hour cycles in a laboratory iron–air battery. Separately, electricity-system models show how longer storage could lower costs and cover seasonal gaps in wind and solar supply.
missing: Installations must repeatedly deliver controllable electricity for weeks and separately recover energy stored across seasons.
Long operation must establish energy losses, equipment life, maintenance needs and dependable output after long idle periods.
Full costs must include charging electricity, conversion equipment and replacement, alongside land and materials.
Measured performance and costs must support cheaper, reliable electricity systems across different regions.

milestones.label: Independent audits confirm weeks of output and seasonal recovery
milestones.explanation: Grid-connected installations would have to repeat both capabilities over years in contrasting climates under independent audit. This would establish dependable performance across operating conditions.

milestones.label: Full costs change the cheapest reliable grid designs
milestones.explanation: Studies using measured performance and full lifetime costs would have to change the cheapest reliable electricity-system designs across regions. This would establish value against competing ways to meet demand.

milestones.label: Seasonal completion requires tests beyond DOE's framework
milestones.explanation: Seasonal storage would have to meet the proposed tests beyond DOE's framework for bringing storage to market. That framework alone does not define when the full capability counts as complete.

uncertain: It remains unclear which storage approach can combine low cost, useful efficiency, long life and widely available materials and sites.
The cost and performance needed to succeed depend on regional resources, reliability needs, financing and how often storage is used.

page.title: Multi-week and seasonal electricity storage
page.definition: Grid electricity storage supplies rated power for multiple weeks and retains energy for electricity recovery months later in another season. Each service reaches a lifetime storage cost of US$0.05 per delivered kilowatt-hour, evaluated at its own cycling frequency.

goal.need: The Royal Society's 2023 hourly model used 37 years of weather data and assumed Great Britain electricity demand of 570 TWh/year. Its central assumptions required about 60–100 TWh of hydrogen storage, measured as fuel energy. A 2024 Western Interconnect model examined 39 scenarios and found seasonal storage operation cost-effective when storage capital costs fell below US$5/kWh.

figures.caption: The Royal Society's model of wind-and-solar electricity supply in Great Britain
figures.note: Hydrogen capacity denotes fuel energy on a lower-heating-value basis. The storage range depends on wind and solar supply.

completion.title: Commercial grid storage provides multi-week discharge and seasonal shifting at US$0.05/kWh of storage.
completion.criterion: Commercial grid-connected installations demonstrate both services. Multi-week discharge supplies rated electrical power continuously for at least 336 hours (14 days). Seasonal shifting returns electricity months after charging, in another season. Each service achieves levelized cost of storage ≤US$0.05/kWh delivered, adapting DOE's 2023 calculation to service-specific cycling and measured performance. Costs cover capital, finance, maintenance, replacement and conversion losses. Charging energy corresponding to recovered output is costed separately. Different technologies may serve the two cases.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas. The 14-day minimum and application of DOE's cost target to both storage services are Atlas criteria.
completion.basis: Searches of DOE Storage Shot and Liftoff documents, ARPA-E DAYS rules, UK LoDES guidance and the Royal Society report found no joint completion criterion for multi-week discharge, seasonal electricity recovery and cost. DOE's target covers 10+ hours. DAYS covers 10 to approximately 100 hours. The Atlas criterion combines the UK programme's temporal scope with DOE's cost target, adapting DOE's daily-cycling assumptions to each service.

milestones.title: Electricity-storage components demonstrate their functions in laboratory tests.
milestones.criterion: Integrated storage components demonstrate feasibility in laboratory testing, meeting DOE technology readiness level (TRL) 4. For multi-week discharge, precursor evidence includes 12.5-hour cycles in laboratory iron–air batteries, reported on 9 November 2022. For seasonal shifting, an Al–Ni laboratory cell retained 92.3% of discharge capacity after 12 weeks at room temperature, measured at 3 mA, reported on 20 April 2022.
milestones.set_by: US Department of Energy, EERE R 540.112-02, general TRL 4 criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: testing in laboratory environment demonstrates the concept.

milestones.title: An electricity-storage system prototype demonstrates engineering feasibility in a relevant environment.
milestones.criterion: A system prototype demonstrates engineering feasibility in an environment relevant to its intended user, meeting DOE TRL 6. Related component results include two Form iron–air modules tested with EPRI verification, with the second delivering about 2.81 kW for 108–110 hours, reported in November 2025. For seasonal hydrogen storage, the 2026 HyDUS report assessed its integrated architecture at TRL 5 and its underlying depleted-uranium storage technology at TRL 6.
milestones.set_by: US Department of Energy, EERE R 540.112-02, general TRL 6 criterion.

milestones.title: A near-full-scale electricity-storage prototype operates in its intended operational environment.
milestones.criterion: A near-full-scale prototype operates with most functions available and ancillary systems integrated, meeting DOE TRL 7. For multi-week-discharge precursors, Form reported more than 10 grid-connected packs and continuous 100-hour duration in 2026. For seasonal shifting, RAG reported two storage cycles on 16 May 2025, including about 500,000 m³ of hydrogen stored for months and subsequent electricity generation. These developer-reported results are not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: US Department of Energy, EERE R 540.112-02, general TRL 7 criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: System prototyping demonstration in operational environment.

milestones.title: A full-scale electricity-storage system passes tests against all end-user specifications.
milestones.criterion: A full-scale electricity-storage system passes simulated and operational tests against all end-user specifications, meeting DOE TRL 8. Qualification applies separately to the two storage services.
milestones.set_by: US Department of Energy, EERE R 540.112-02, general TRL 8 pre-commercial demonstration criterion.

not_found: No public TRL 8 assessment for either listed service was located among the cited development projects.
Tang's repository abstract gives no cell count, and its linked accepted manuscript could not be fetched.
The CEC-hosted Dowling paper supplied with the draft could not be fetched.
A numerical round-trip efficiency for the Form modules was unavailable in the public project report.
RAG's release gives no gas-volume reference conditions, round-trip efficiency or storage cost.

results.finding: One laboratory solid-oxide iron–air cell completed multiple 12.5-hour cycles.
results.detail: The integrated cell demonstrates laboratory cycling, but the reported cycle duration is a precursor to multi-week discharge; the paper does not establish DOE TRL 4 for that service.
results.quote:
Finally, by combining an improved RSOC with the
Ir-catalyzed Fe-bed, we demonstrate the LDES performance
with multiple stable 12.5 hour charge/discharge cycles on an
f100 size SOIAB.

results.finding: Al–Ni laboratory cell, sample size not stated: 92.3% capacity retention after 12 weeks.
results.detail: The presentation reports the specified retention and duration but does not state the storage temperature or measurement current, so it does not establish all conditions in the criterion.

results.finding: Two Form iron–air prototype modules were tested; the second discharged for 108–110 hours.
results.detail: EPRI independently analyzed performance data. Testing used a module in a stand with representative auxiliary systems, rather than an integrated system prototype; the report does not establish DOE TRL 6.

results.finding: One grid-connected iron–air pilot demonstrated 100-hour storage.
results.detail: The pilot operated in a utility laboratory under real-world grid conditions, but the source does not demonstrate multi-week discharge or state a DOE TRL assessment.
results.quote:
Ore Energy has successfully concluded a grid-connected pilot of its 100-hour iron-air long-duration energy storage (LDES) system at
EDF R&D Laboratories
in Écuelles, France, demonstrating multi-day storage performance in a real utility environment.

results.finding: One integrated hydrogen power-to-power prototype achieved 13% system-level round-trip efficiency.
results.detail: The prototype operated at UCI using customer demand and renewable-generation profiles, and its storage tanks were monitored idle for 12 months. The report does not establish electricity recovery after months of storage or explicitly assess the system at TRL 6.
results.quote:
The combined electrolyzer-to-fuel cell round-trip efficiency was measured at 13 percent on a 
system level, with observed optimization pathways targeting up to 32 percent improvement, 
including through rightsizing chiller systems, operating at partial load, and enhancing thermal 
integration across subsystems.

results.finding: RAG's USS 2030 demonstration completed two hydrogen storage cycles.
results.detail: RAG also reports storing approximately 500,000 m³ of hydrogen for several months and using the recovered hydrogen to generate electricity in its combined heat and power plant.
results.quote: The project operation, consisting of two storage cycles, has been successfully completed.
